title: Grade 10 English — Modals & Determiners and Clauses
description: Modals and Determiners and Clauses practice questions
subject: english

questions.question: Choose the correct modal: You ___ see a doctor if you're feeling unwell.
questions.explanation: 'Should' expresses advice or recommendation. 'You should see a doctor' gives a strong suggestion.

questions.question: 'You must not smoke here.' This modal expresses:
questions.explanation: 'Must not' expresses strong prohibition (something is not allowed). Example: 'You must not enter without permission.'

questions.question: Which modal expresses possibility or probability in the future?
questions.explanation: 'May' (stronger possibility) and 'might' (weaker possibility) express that something is possible. 'It may rain today' = there is a possibility of rain.

questions.question: Fill in: When I was young, I ___ climb trees easily. (past ability)
questions.explanation: 'Could' is used for past ability. 'I could climb trees' means I had the ability to do so in the past. 'Can' is for present ability.

questions.question: Choose the correct determiner: I have ___ money left.
questions.explanation: 'Little/a little' is used with uncountable nouns (money). 'Few/a few' is used with countable nouns. 'A little' (positive) = some; 'little' (negative) = hardly any.

questions.question: '___ student passed the exam.' Which determiner is correct for a specific student?
questions.explanation: 'The' is the definite article, used when referring to a specific or already known person/thing. 'The student' refers to a particular student.

questions.question: The modal 'would' is used to express:
questions.explanation: 'Would' is used for habitual/repeated actions in the past: 'When I was young, I would go to the park every Sunday.' It can also express polite requests and hypothetical situations.

questions.question: '___ sugar do you take in your tea?' — Which interrogative determiner fits?
questions.explanation: 'How much' is used with uncountable nouns (sugar, water, money). 'How many' is for countable nouns (apples, students).

questions.question: A noun clause acts as a:
options: Noun (subject or object) in a sentence
questions.explanation: A noun clause functions as a noun — it can be the subject, object, or complement. Example: 'What she said is true.' ('What she said' is the subject.)

questions.question: Identify the adjective clause: 'The boy who won the race is my friend.'
questions.explanation: 'who won the race' is an adjective (relative) clause modifying 'the boy'. It begins with the relative pronoun 'who' and describes which boy.

questions.question: An adverb clause of condition usually begins with:
questions.explanation: Adverb clauses of condition begin with subordinating conjunctions: if, unless, provided that, in case. Example: 'Unless you study, you will not pass.'

questions.question: Identify the type of clause: 'I will call you when I arrive.'
questions.explanation: 'When I arrive' is an adverb clause of time, modifying the verb 'will call'. 'When' is the subordinating conjunction.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options: He works hard so he succeeds.
The book that I borrowed was excellent.
If it rains, we will stay home.
questions.explanation: 'that I borrowed' is a relative (adjective) clause modifying 'The book'. Relative clauses begin with relative pronouns: who, which, that, whom, whose.

questions.question: A main (independent) clause:
options: Cannot stand alone as a sentence
Can stand alone as a complete sentence
questions.explanation: A main (independent) clause has a subject and predicate and can stand alone as a complete sentence. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone — it depends on the main clause.

questions.question: Identify the noun clause: 'I believe that honesty is the best policy.'
options: that honesty is the best policy
questions.explanation: 'that honesty is the best policy' is a noun clause functioning as the object of 'believe'. It answers the question 'what do I believe?'
